nodes.gloss: This means drifting through life without any goal or direction, taking each day as it comes, committing to nothing, and having no sense of what one is working toward.

nodes.label: alcoholic
nodes.gloss: An alcoholic is someone who cannot stop drinking: hiding bottles, counting drinks and lying about the count, shaking in the morning until the first one, losing jobs, licenses, and people over it, and swearing off, then going back.

nodes.label: aloof
nodes.gloss: This means being aloof: cool and distant, unmoved by charm or banter, and giving off no warmth that anyone would read as interest or invitation.

nodes.label: balanced
nodes.gloss: This means being balanced in one's attention: giving each part of a topic its due weight, making a point once and moving on, and never fixating on any one detail.

nodes.label: brilliant
nodes.gloss: This means being brilliant, never dim-witted: quick and deep at once, grasping a hard idea on first hearing, seeing the connection others miss, and getting to the answer fast.

nodes.label: chattering
nodes.gloss: This means talking on and on in a quick, easy stream, filling every pause with small remarks, asides and passing thoughts, and rarely letting a silence settle.

nodes.label: clandestine
nodes.gloss: This means keeping one's plans, dealings and sources hidden from others as a settled habit, choosing covert action by default even when openness would serve just as well.

nodes.label: concealing
nodes.gloss: This means keeping a secret or hidden purpose from others, withholding its true nature and steering conversations away from anything that would reveal it.

nodes.label: crude
nodes.gloss: This means speaking and joking in a coarse, vulgar way, with rough language and crude humor, and showing no concern for polish or refinement in one's manner.

nodes.label: declining
nodes.gloss: This means living with failing health or strength year after year: needing more help with ordinary tasks, tiring quickly, and speaking often of what the body can no longer do.

nodes.label: deft
nodes.gloss: This means handling tasks with a quick, skilled touch, working with one's hands in a way that is precise, nimble and easy to watch.

nodes.label: delinquent
nodes.gloss: A delinquent is a teenager in trouble with the law: skipping school, shoplifting, tagging walls, breaking into cars, running with a crew that does the same, on a first-name basis with the juvenile court, and not planning to change.

nodes.label: derisive
nodes.gloss: This means mocking others with scorn, treating their ideas, efforts and failings as objects to ridicule rather than to take seriously.

nodes.label: disgruntled
nodes.gloss: This means being disgruntled, never job-satisfied: resenting the work, the boss, the pay and the hours, airing fresh grievances every shift, and sure the place owes one better. The opposite of job-satisfied.

nodes.label: disheveled
nodes.gloss: This means going about with hair uncombed, shirts untucked and clothes rumpled, seldom checking one's appearance and not minding who notices.

nodes.label: disobedient
nodes.gloss: This means refusing to follow instructions or rules one is given, setting them aside in favor of one's own judgment and acting against them when they conflict with it.

nodes.label: estranged
nodes.gloss: An estranged person is someone cut off for years from their own family: not speaking to a parent, a sibling, or a grown child, skipping holidays and funerals, hearing their news secondhand, and carrying the old fight wherever they go.

nodes.label: flattering
nodes.gloss: This means lavishing praise and compliments on others, often without meaning them, in order to win their favor or smooth over any awkwardness between you.

nodes.label: homeless
nodes.gloss: A homeless person is someone with no place to live: sleeping in a car, a tent, or a doorway, carrying everything in a bag, finding somewhere to wash and charge a phone, and lining up early for a shelter bed.

nodes.label: incorruptible
nodes.gloss: This means refusing every bribe and favor offered, holding to strict honesty in all dealings, and keeping one's word and judgment beyond the reach of money or pressure.

nodes.label: insulting
nodes.gloss: This means habitually mocking, demeaning and belittling the people one speaks to, using cutting remarks to make them feel small and foolish.

nodes.label: intemperate
nodes.gloss: This means being intemperate: no stoic composure and no restraint, giving feelings free rein, flaring up at provocation, gushing at good news, despairing at bad, and never accepting a loss quietly.

nodes.label: irrestrainable
nodes.gloss: This means acting on impulse with no brake on one's conduct, letting desire, anger, or whim carry one forward regardless of consequences, and treating self-control as something one never bothers to practice.

nodes.label: jumpy
nodes.gloss: This means being easily startled and keeping a nervous edge, so that sudden noises, movements, or unexpected news set one on alert as a matter of temperament.

nodes.label: just
nodes.gloss: This means giving everyone what they deserve: the bigger share to whoever did more, nothing to the freeloader, favors returned in kind, and the punishment fitted to the offense.

nodes.label: kind
nodes.gloss: This means being kind: going out of one's way for people, doing the small favor unasked, finding the warm word, and leaving everyone feeling better for it.

nodes.label: malleable
nodes.gloss: This means easily shifting one's opinions, plans and loyalties to match whoever is speaking most forcefully, yielding to pressure from others rather than holding a firm position of one's own.

nodes.label: maniacal
nodes.gloss: This means acting with a wild, frenzied intensity, laughing, shouting and lunging as though one has lost all hold on reason and self-control.

nodes.label: masochistic
nodes.gloss: This means finding pleasure in one's own pain or humiliation, seeking out suffering and degradation and taking satisfaction from being hurt or belittled.

nodes.label: mean
nodes.gloss: This means being mean: going out of one's way to put people down, refusing the small favor, finding the snide word, and leaving everyone feeling worse for it.

nodes.label: meddling
nodes.gloss: This means prying into other people's business, asking pointed questions about their private lives, and inserting oneself into decisions that are none of one's concern.

nodes.label: meek
nodes.gloss: This means being meek: speaking softly and apologetically, never talking back, taking a rebuke in silence, and never sassy, shrinking from anything that sounds like cheek or attitude.

nodes.label: minimizing
nodes.gloss: This means playing down problems, mistakes and setbacks, treating them as smaller than they are and telling others not to worry about what has gone wrong.

nodes.label: morose
nodes.gloss: This means keeping a sullen, dour mood and withdrawing into silence, showing little willingness to talk and answering others, when one answers at all, with grudging short replies.

nodes.label: nosy
nodes.gloss: This means prying into other people's private affairs, asking about their finances, relationships and personal matters, and feeling entitled to know what they keep to themselves.

nodes.label: obscene
nodes.gloss: This means speaking in a crudely lewd manner, using sexually offensive language and innuendo that shocks or disgusts those who hear it.

nodes.label: overdiligent
nodes.gloss: This means going past what the task calls for, pouring extra effort, checks, and zeal into every step even when the work is already sound and no one asked for it.

nodes.label: overmasculine
nodes.gloss: This means acting out macho swagger at every turn, dominating conversations and people, bragging of toughness, treating aggression as strength, and answering any hint of softness with scorn or a show of force.

nodes.label: overstepping
nodes.gloss: This means going beyond the authority one has been given, making decisions and taking actions that belong to others and crossing proper limits as a matter of habit.

nodes.label: parasitic
nodes.gloss: This means living off other people's labor, resources, or goodwill while taking what one can and giving nothing back in return.

nodes.label: pathetic
nodes.gloss: This means being consistently feeble and inadequate in one's conduct and character, falling short in ways that earn contempt rather than sympathy from those around one.

nodes.label: phony
nodes.gloss: This means putting on a show of warmth, interest, or expertise one does not actually feel or have, and presenting a false self to others as though it were genuine.

nodes.label: prudish
nodes.gloss: This means being easily shocked by sexual or bodily matters, recoiling from frank talk about them and treating open mention of such things as improper or offensive.

nodes.label: purposive
nodes.gloss: This means keeping one's actions aimed at clearly chosen goals, so that each step is taken with a definite intent rather than drifting or reacting without direction.

nodes.label: repressed
nodes.gloss: This means keeping one's feelings locked away, holding them in and refusing to let them show even when they press hard for expression.

nodes.label: resigned
nodes.gloss: This means quietly accepting an unwelcome situation as it stands, letting go of the urge to fight it or push back against what cannot be changed.

nodes.label: restrainable
nodes.gloss: This means accepting correction and limits without resistance, staying calm and cooperative when others move to hold one in check.

nodes.label: rugged
nodes.gloss: This means facing hardship without complaint, enduring discomfort and setbacks through one's own resilience, and handling problems alone rather than leaning on others for help.

nodes.label: self-sacrificing
nodes.gloss: This means giving up one's own comfort, chances or safety for one's family, team or country: eating last, taking the worst shift or the dangerous job, so that they come through.

nodes.label: sulky
nodes.gloss: This means going quiet and withdrawn after a slight, answering questions in clipped words, avoiding eye contact, and nursing resentment long after the matter has been settled.

nodes.label: unceremonious
nodes.gloss: This means skipping ceremony and protocol: getting straight to the matter without the customary forms or order of proceedings, and doing things whichever way is handiest, however they have always been done.

nodes.label: undiplomatic
nodes.gloss: This means being undiplomatic: saying the awkward thing in the room, naming the fault in front of everyone, ignoring who will be offended, and treating tact as a waste of time.

nodes.label: unladylike
nodes.gloss: This means behaving rudely, coarsely and boisterously, with loud talk, crude jokes and rough manners that flout genteel expectations for women and never bother to hide it.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve taking the person seriously, but attentive listening is about accurately attending and responding to what a speaker said, while engaged is about caring about outcomes and stakes; each can occur without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve drawing others in through warmth and charm, but 'attracting' emphasizes engaging company that people seek out, while 'adorable' emphasizes being endearing and lovable; each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Attracting is about drawing others toward oneself through warmth and charm, while gregarious is about oneself actively seeking out company; they share a social-warmth core but point in opposite directions and neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both concern emotions, but the target is perceiving and responding to others' moods, while the other is expressing or discussing feelings, so each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve emotional awareness of others and caring responses, but attunement stresses perceiving unspoken mood shifts while empathy stresses understanding, compassion and warmth more broadly, so each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both centre on emotional awareness answered with care. Attunement stresses perceptiveness to unspoken mood shifts, while empathy stresses compassionate understanding of feelings and perspectives more broadly, so each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: One is perceptive sensitivity to others' moods and responding with care, the other is being strongly and lastingly affected by interpersonal events; both concern emotional responsiveness to people, but perception and care differ from intense, lingering reactivity.

reasons.opus: Both direct attention toward others, but one centres on perceiving emotional undercurrents and the other on making conversation about others' affairs and needs, so each can exist without the other.

reasons.opus: Both centre on the expectation that things will turn out well. Auspicious is an aura of luck that others pick up on, while optimistic is a person's own hopeful outlook and positive framing, so neither implies the other.

reasons.opus: Both describe responding without deliberation, but automatic stresses habitual reflex while reactive stresses responding in the moment instead of planning ahead, so each adds something the other lacks.

Catechizing is a specific teaching method of drilling set questions and memorized answers on the faith, while religious is a general orientation of drawing on faith in thinking and deciding; they share a religious domain but are different concepts.

Catechizing is a teaching method of fixed question-and-answer drilling, while orthodox is a doctrinal stance of adhering to accepted belief; they are related in religious transmission but neither implies the other.

Catechizing is teaching religious doctrine through fixed question-and-answer drills, while unchallenging is accepting what others say without pushback; they concern different things, with only a loose link in rote, non-questioning exchange.

Categorical is about how one speaks (flat, unqualified assertions), whereas closure-seeking is a psychological need for settled answers and intolerance of ambiguity; they overlap in firmness but neither implies the other.
Both involve leaving no hedging or openness, but categorical is about flat, unqualified assertions of claims, while decisive is about choosing and committing to a course of action.
Both concern deep intimacy and sharing life without reserve, but cater-cousin is about one dearest companion while close-knit is about a whole circle of family and old friends.
reasons.opus: Both describe intimate bonds where people share everything. The target is one dyadic dearest friendship, while close-knit is a tight group of family and friends, so each has something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Cathartic is about helping others release pent-up emotion, whereas expressive is about openly showing one's own feelings; both concern emotional outpouring, but in different directions and neither implies the other.

Cathartic is about helping others release pent-up emotions and feel lighter, while emotional is about general expression or awareness of feelings; they share the emotion domain but neither implies the other.

Both involve fixating on small slights, but cattish adds malicious backbiting and watching others, while petty is about blowing trivial issues out of proportion without necessarily being spiteful or gossipy.
Both involve malice toward others, but cattish is petty backbiting and watchfulness, while spiteful here is self-costly sabotage to deny a rival; neither implies the other.
Both involve hostility toward others, but cattish is covert petty gossip and spite behind backs, while quarrelsome is open confrontation, stubbornness in argument, grudge-holding and quick anger.
Both involve ill will toward others, but cattish is petty backbiting and spite while malicious is broader deliberate harm, deceit, and manipulation, so each includes things the other lacks.
Both involve habitual malicious remarks, but cattish is covert backbiting and petty spite behind people's backs, while insulting is direct demeaning of people to their faces.

Both involve a hostile attitude toward others, but cattish is specifically petty backbiting and spite, while antagonistic is a broad low-agreeableness cluster (distrust, manipulation, selfishness, combativeness, coldness) that only partly overlaps via fault-finding.
Both involve cutting remarks, but catty is malicious gossip about absent people while sarcastic is ironic mockery of anyone, often to their face; they share only the sharp-tongued core.

Both involve taking pleasure in others' misfortune with ill will, but catty is specifically sly verbal backbiting about absent people, while malicious is a broader intent to harm, deceive or manipulate by any means.
reasons.opus: Both involve ill will and taking pleasure in others' misfortune, but catty means petty, sly verbal digs behind people's backs, while malicious means a broader, deliberate drive to harm, deceive or manipulate, and neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve sly, indirect digs, but catty is malicious gossip about absent people with glee at their failures, while passive-aggressive is indirect expression of hostility or disapproval, typically to the person's face, and without the gossip or gloating.
reasons.opus: Both involve indirect, sly hostility, but catty is malicious gossip about absent people, while passive-aggressive is covert hostility usually aimed at the person present; each has elements the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve cutting, biting remarks, but catty is specifically malicious gossip about absent people with glee at their failures, while acerbic is sharp, harsh wit that need not be backbiting or directed at absent targets.
reasons.opus: Both involve cutting remarks, but catty centres on malicious talk about absent people and pleasure in their failures, while acerbic is harsh, witty criticism in general, possibly said to someone's face and without malice.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve cutting remarks, but catty is malicious gossip about absent people with glee at their failures, while sardonic is dry, cynical ironic mockery aimed at situations or society broadly.

Both involve ill will toward others, but catty is specifically sly, malicious talk about absent people and pleasure in their small failures, while malevolent is a broader, deeper hostility that includes working toward harm; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both involve ill will toward others, but catty is petty, sly verbal sniping behind people's backs, while malevolent is a deep hostility that actively works toward others' harm. Neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve deliberately harming others, but the target is instrumental harm for personal gain, while malicious is harm pursued for its own sake or for satisfaction; neither implies the other.
Both involve harming others in pursuit of one's aims, but 'harmful' is broader (includes negligence and enabling others), while the target is specifically deliberate harm for personal advancement.

Both involve deliberately harming others, but the target harms for personal gain while spite harms at a cost to oneself with no gain, so the motives are nearly opposite even though the harm is shared.
Both involve deliberately harming others, but the target is instrumental harm for personal gain while evil is gratuitous cruelty and delight in suffering; each lacks what the other has.

Both involve deliberately harming others, but the target harms instrumentally for personal advancement and is indifferent to the injury, while the killer's goal is the victim's distress itself in a gaming context.

Both involve deliberately harming others, but the target is instrumental harm for personal gain (indifference to injury), while malevolence is harm driven by hostility and ill will for its own sake; neither implies the other.
Both involve harming others, but the target is deliberate harm as a means to personal gain, while malign is general harmfulness to others, by design or chance, with no self-serving motive required.

Both involve putting oneself ahead of others, but selfishness is a general self-prioritizing and need not involve deliberately harming others, while causing harm for advantage is an active, deliberate form that goes beyond mere self-focus.
Both involve yielding to others, but caving is a reaction to intense pressure while submissiveness is a general readiness to defer without needing pressure; each adds something the other lacks.

Both involve giving up one's stance for others, but caving is a reactive yielding to forceful pressure, while accommodating is a general, willing readiness to adjust to others' needs without needing pressure.
Both involve accommodating others, but agreeableness is forgiving, lenient, cooperative and even-tempered, while caving under pressure is yielding to forceful demands; neither implies the other.
Both involve yielding to others, but caving is capitulating to forceful pressure, while deference is respectful yielding to authority or expertise without any pressure needed.

Agreeableness is a broad trait including yielding in quarrels, which partly overlaps with caving under pressure, but it also covers trust, helpfulness, modesty and compassion, while caving is specifically capitulating to forceful pressure.

Caving under pressure is yielding to forceful demands, while face culture is a broader orientation toward social standing, harmony and saving face; they may co-occur through conflict avoidance, but neither implies the other.

Both involve fixating on trivial matters, but caviling is habitual nitpicking at proposals and work, while pettiness is about minor grievances and slights blown out of proportion; each has features the other lacks.

Both involve fixating on minor details, but the caviler raises objections to nearly everything put before them, while the pedant is over-concerned with technicalities and rules without necessarily objecting; each has something the other lacks.
Both involve sexual restraint, but celibate is a behavioral commitment to abstain from sex, while chaste as described is a purity of thought, speech and desire; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both centre on sexual abstinence, but celibacy is a standing behavioural commitment that can coexist with desire, while chastity here is inner purity of thought and speech without any vow implied.

reasons.sonnet: Celibacy is a committed choice to abstain from sex, while asexuality is a lack of sexual attraction; they often coincide in outcome but one is behavior/commitment and the other is orientation, so each can exist without the other.
Celibacy is abstaining from sex specifically, while asceticism is a broader denial of pleasures and comforts for spiritual ends; celibacy can be one expression of it, but neither implies the other.
Celibate is a personal commitment to abstain from sex, while puritanical is a broad moralistic condemnation of many vices in oneself and others; they share only a loose link to sexual restraint.

Both concern communal living, but a cenobite's life is a chosen religious community under a rule, whereas Gemeinschaft is an inborn, kin-based belonging, so they are neighbouring but distinct concepts.

Both involve keeping certain content or voices out of view, but censorial is actively vetting and suppressing material judged objectionable, while exclusionary is favoring mainstream voices and leaving others out, so each has an aspect the other lacks.
Both involve withholding content before it reaches others, but censoring is removing others' material as a job, while guarded is self-restraint in one's own speech out of caution.

Censoring is actively removing objectionable content before it reaches an audience, while exclusionary is leaving out non-mainstream voices; both limit what is heard, but one is content removal and the other is group-based omission.
Both involve formal dignity in conduct, but ceremonious stresses strict protocol and ritual, while dignified stresses poise, composure and self-respect; neither implies the other.

Both involve dignified, proper conduct, but ceremonious stresses strict adherence to protocol and ritual in behavior, while formal as described centers on professional, grammatically proper language and tone; each adds something the other lacks.
Both involve formal dignity and gravitas, but ceremonious stresses strict protocol and etiquette while serious stresses avoiding humor and focusing on substance; neither implies the other.
Both involve formal dignity, but ceremonious centers on strict adherence to protocol while solemn centers on a grave, sober disposition that rarely jokes; each can occur without the other.

Both suggest a formal, conventional manner, but ceremonious is about strict protocol and dignified conduct, while staid is about settled respectability and avoiding controversy or offense; neither implies the other.

Both involve strict attention to form and procedure, but ceremonious is about formal dignified conduct and protocol, while formalist prioritizes structure and format over substance, so each adds something the other lacks.

Both involve treating one's views as settled and dismissing challenges, though closed-mindedness stresses refusing to consider alternatives while certainty stresses confidence in being right; they largely overlap and differ in emphasis.
reasons.opus: Both describe treating one's views as unquestionable fact and rejecting challenges; closed-minded stresses refusing to consider evidence and alternatives, while the target stresses never doubting one's own correctness, so they differ mainly in emphasis.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve unyielding firmness, but one is epistemic certainty about being right while the other is behavioral inflexibility about methods and plans; each can occur without the other.
Both involve never questioning one's own assumptions, but one is about conviction of being right while the other is about rigid fixation on a single approach, and each can occur without the other.

Both involve standing firm against challenge, but the target is an epistemic conviction of being right, while unyielding is a behavioral refusal to concede that can occur without believing oneself infallible.

Both involve firm views, but certainty of own rightness is about epistemic closure to being wrong, while opinionated is about taking and pushing positions on everything; one can have either without the other.

Both treat their views as settled and any departure as error, but the target is self-certainty about one's own judgments while orthodox is adherence to received doctrine and authority; either can exist without the other.

Both involve confident belief in being right, but the target is general infallibility about one's own views, while exclusivism specifically asserts one school or way is right and treats rivals as errors; each can occur without the other.
Both involve rigid conviction, but one is personal infallibility about one's own views while the other is belief in universal, exceptionless principles; neither implies the other.

Both involve holding firmly to settled conclusions, but certainty of rightness is about belief in one's own infallibility while closure-seeking is about needing resolution and discomfort with ambiguity; either can occur without the other.

Chaffering is haggling over prices and pushing back on offers, while unyielding is a general refusal to give ground in any matter; they share some firmness in negotiation but neither implies the other (a haggler may concede in the end, an unyielding person need not haggle).
Both involve getting a lower price, but chaffering is negotiating each price directly while bargain-hunting is seeking sales, coupons and comparisons; a person can do either without the other.
Chaffering is specifically haggling over prices, while disagreeableness is a general contrariness in dealing with people; they share a bit of pushing back but differ in domain and motive.

Both involve forceful pushing for one's aims, but chaffering is specifically hard bargaining over prices, while aggression is a broad combative stance that rejects compromise, which haggling actually involves.
Haggling hard over prices is about bargaining and negotiation, while rigidity is about inflexibly sticking to one way of doing things; they share only a loose sense of stubbornness.
Both involve shifting opinions to fit others, but the chameleon adapts to whoever is present as social camouflage, while the malleable person yields to forceful pressure; neither implies the other.

Both involve adjusting opinions and manner to the audience, but 'performative' centres on managing impressions and can be consistent, while 'chameleon' centres on shifting views to match each company.

Both involve adjusting positions to others, but chameleon is about mirroring each audience's views (often inauthentically), while accommodating is about yielding to meet needs and keep peace; neither implies the other.

Both involve adjusting to different audiences, but chameleon means changing stated opinions to please whoever is present, while adaptable here means adjusting tone, detail and format without necessarily changing views, so each adds something the other lacks.

Both involve bending one's views to please others, but the chameleon shifts with every audience while the sycophant flatters and over-agrees with a particular person, so each has a part the other lacks.

Both involve adjusting tone and manner to the person or occasion, but chameleonic means reshaping one's whole character to fit whoever is present, while adaptable (as described) is a deliberate adjustment of communication style, with no loss of a stable self.
reasons.opus: Both adjust tone and manner to the person at hand, but chameleonic reshapes one's very character to mirror others, while adaptable tailors communication for the listener's benefit without any change of self.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve adapting manner to the audience, but chameleonic is shifting to match whoever is present, while performative is strategic impression management that may not mean matching others; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both describe adjusting manner to suit each audience, but chameleonic is an identity that shifts to match others, while performative is deliberate impression management aimed at a desired image; neither requires the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve shifting according to other people, but chameleonic is adapting personality and manner to the company, whereas malleable is yielding opinions and loyalties to forceful pressure.
reasons.opus: Both involve reshaping oneself to match others, but chameleonic concerns one's manner and personality across social settings, while malleable concerns giving up opinions and loyalties under forceful pressure, so a persona can have either without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve adjusting to other people, but chameleonic is shifting personality and manner to fit each company, while accommodating is yielding positions and approach to meet needs and keep the peace; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both involve adapting to others, but chameleonic is shifting one's personality to mirror company, while accommodating is yielding positions to meet others' needs and keep the peace.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve adjusting opinions and manner to the audience, but chameleonlike is conformity to whoever is present, while performative is strategic impression management that need not mean agreeing with others.

Both involve adjusting one's stance to others, but chameleonlike is shifting to seem to agree with whoever is present, while accommodating is giving way to meet others' needs and keep the peace; each adds something the other lacks.

Chameleonlike is about shifting opinions and manner to match each audience, while sly (HEXACO) is about manipulative self-interest, flattery, rule-breaking and entitlement; flattery overlaps slightly but neither implies the other.

Both involve insincere, audience-pleasing talk, but chameleonlike is about shifting opinions and manner to match each person, while glib is about smooth, ready, superficial charm, so each has something the other lacks.

Both involve excessive agreeableness to win approval, but chameleonlike means shifting opinions and manner to match whoever is present, while sycophantic means flattering and deferring to a particular person; neither implies the other.

Both involve a focus on winning and excelling, but 'champ' is pride and quiet confidence in consistently being a top performer, while 'competitive' is a drive to outdo others and frame things as contests; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both center on winning, but champ is the pride and confident bearing of someone who already excels, while competitive is the drive to beat others and treat situations as contests; neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve concern with winning and looking competent, but champ is quiet pride in genuinely excelling, while performance-oriented is a goal orientation of proving ability, choosing safe wins and favoring scores over learning; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both centre on achievement and showing excellence, but champ is about pride and confidence from consistently winning, while performance-oriented is about a motivational style of seeking safe wins and scores rather than learning; neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve quiet confidence, but champ centers on pride in winning and top performance while self-assured centers on secure self-worth and independence from others' approval; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both involve confidence, but champ centres on pride in winning and excelling, while self-assured is a secure sense of one's worth that needs no achievement; each has what the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve a drive to excel and win, but champ is about confident pride in being a top performer, while Bartle's achiever is about accumulating points, levels and rank in a game as the goal.
reasons.opus: Both centre on pride in high achievement and winning. Champ is a general self-assured excellence, while achiever is a goal-driven motivation focused on game points and rank, so neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve holding firm without wavering under pressure, but 'champion' is about publicly advocating a cause, while 'unyielding' is about refusing to give ground in personal disagreements; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both involve holding firm under pressure, but championing is public advocacy for a cause, while unyielding is interpersonal refusal to concede one's position, so each has something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve steadfastly standing by something at personal cost, but champion is public advocacy of a cause while loyal is faithfulness to people, secrets and sides, so each has features the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both involve steadfast commitment despite cost, but championing is publicly advocating a cause while loyalty is faithfulness to people; neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve strongly advocating positions, but championing is steadfast, costly defense of a particular cause, while opinionated is holding and voicing firm views on every topic without necessarily sacrificing anything.

Both involve fervent, unwavering devotion to a cause, but 'champion' stresses steadfast public defense at personal cost, while 'zealous' stresses hot, crusading passion and distrust of coolness; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both describe ardent commitment to causes, but championing stresses steadfast public defence while zealotry stresses heated fervour and crusading temperament, so each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve firm, unwavering advocacy for a side, but champion is principled defense of a cause at personal cost, while partisan is tribal loyalty to a political side with bad-faith readings of opponents; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both involve firm, committed advocacy. Champion is principled public defense of a cause at personal cost, while partisan is tribal loyalty to a political side with closed-minded dismissal of opponents, so each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve conviction, but championing is steadfast public advocacy of a cause at personal cost, while confidence is general self-assured certainty in statements, so each has something the other lacks.

Both involve steadfast conviction, but championing is publicly advocating and defending a cause, while principled is consistently following an ethical framework in decisions; neither implies the other.
Changeling is a folkloric identity of being a fairy-substituted child, while ethereal is a delicate, otherworldly manner of communicating; both evoke the fairy realm but are different concepts.

Both involve transformation, but the target is about reshaping external things and measuring work by change made, while the other is about repeatedly remaking oneself; they share a core of change-orientation but differ in object.

Both involve transforming things, but 'changer' is reshaping whatever one finds and measuring work by what has changed, while 'world-changing' is about bending surroundings to one's aims and solving obstacles; they share a core without implying each other.
reasons.opus: Both are about actively altering things. The target is transformation as a way of life, valued for the change itself. World-changing is goal-directed reshaping of one's surroundings to suit one's aims and solve problems. They share a core, but each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve working with whatever is at hand, but the changer's core is transformation as a goal and measure of work, while resourcefulness is improvising around missing means; neither implies the other.

Both involve restraint and acting only when asked, but the target is about limiting edits to the requested scope while the other is about not supervising or intervening in others' work, so they are distinct neighbours.

Both involve holding to principles at a cost, but 'character' is broad reliability and moral firmness, while 'honorable' is specifically a code of absolute prohibitions that rejects ends-justify-means reasoning; honorable is a narrower, more specific form.
reasons.opus: Both centre on holding to principles at personal cost, but honorable adds a strict ends-don't-justify-means absolutism, while character stresses being reliable in word and conduct.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve holding to moral principles consistently rather than convenience, though 'character' adds reliability and willingness to bear costs, while 'principled' stresses an explicit ethical framework and rule-based decisions.
reasons.opus: Both describe steadfast adherence to moral principles over convenience; character adds an emphasis on reliability and enduring personal cost, while principled stresses a consistent stated framework.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve steadfast integrity and reliability under pressure, but incorruptible is narrower, focused on resisting bribes and favors, while character is broader principled conduct.
reasons.opus: Incorruptible is a narrower form of character: holding firm to principle and keeping one's word, here specifically against bribes and pressure.

reasons.sonnet: Both concern moral rightness, but 'character' stresses steadfast principle and reliability under cost, while 'good' stresses benevolence, gladness at others' success, and dissuading wrongdoing; each has elements the other lacks.

Character is personal integrity and reliability in acting on one's principles even at a cost, while absolutism is the belief that principles are universal and exceptionless; both involve firm principles but one is about conduct and the other about the scope of moral claims, and neither implies the other.

Both describe adherence to right conduct even when costly or convenient to abandon, so they share a core; 'character' adds reliability and firmness of word, while 'moral' stresses sensitivity to right and wrong and refusing wrongdoing.
reasons.opus: Both describe doing right and refusing wrong even when it costs or would pay off; character adds an emphasis on steadfast reliability, while moral stresses an inner sense of right and wrong.

reasons.sonnet: Both assume good intent until shown otherwise, but charitable judgment is about interpreting ambiguous words or actions generously, while trusting is a broader expectation of decency and taking motives at face value, so each adds something the other lacks.

Both are generous attitudes toward others' faults, but charitable judgment is about interpreting unclear behavior with good intent beforehand, while forgiving is about pardoning wrongs and releasing resentment afterward.

Both are generous toward others, but charitable judgment is about assuming good intent in ambiguous cases, while magnanimity is about overlooking slights and crediting rivals; each can occur without the other.

They share a core of lenient, generous judgment of others, but agreeableness adds forgiveness, cooperation and temper control, while charitable judgment is specifically about assuming good intent in ambiguous situations.

Both involve going easy on others, but charitable judgment is about assuming good intent in ambiguous cases, while leniency is about low standards and comforting rather than pushing; neither implies the other.

Both involve being kind rather than harsh toward others, and 'slow to judge harshly' touches charitable judgment, but gentleness is about mild, soft manner and restraint in delivery, while charitable judgment is about assuming good intent in ambiguous cases.

Both involve goodwill toward others, but charitable judgment is about interpreting ambiguous behavior generously, while friendliness is about warm outward manner; a person can have either without the other.
Both involve faking something one lacks, but charlatan is specifically feigned expertise, while phony is broader false self-presentation that also covers faked warmth or interest.

Both involve false self-presentation, but the charlatan fakes expertise to cover real gaps in ability, while the pretentious person puts on airs of culture or importance and disdains plainness; neither implies the other.

Both involve misrepresentation and projecting false confidence while hiding limitations, but charlatan is specifically faking expertise, while dishonest as described is a broader strategic presentation of information (omission, avoiding other viewpoints) not limited to faked skill.
Both involve misleading others, but charlatan is specifically faking expertise while deceitful is a general tendency to lie and misrepresent; neither implies the other.

Both involve covering knowledge gaps with false confidence, but the charlatan deliberately feigns expertise for self-presentation, while the confabulator invents plausible details to fill gaps, without necessarily claiming expertise.
Both involve warmth and ease with people, but charmer adds humor and deliberate winning-over, while friendly is general goodwill and approachability without that appeal.
reasons.opus: Both share warm, sociable openness, but a charmer actively wins people over with humor and appeal, while friendly is simply goodwill toward others; each can occur without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve drawing people in through personal appeal, but charmer centers on warmth, humor and putting others at ease, while charismatic emphasizes magnetic confidence and compelling influence, so each has something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both describe drawing people in through personal appeal, but the charmer works through warmth and interest in others while the charismatic works through magnetic confidence and persuasive presence, so each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve warmth and pleasantness toward others, but charming stresses a winning, polished manner that makes one agreeable company, while friendly stresses goodwill and openness rather than suspicion; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both involve warmth and pleasant sociability, but charming stresses a winning, agreeable manner while friendly stresses goodwill and openness toward others, and either can exist without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve light conversational tone, but charming is about winning, agreeable manner toward others, while lighthearted is a disposition of breezy, joking unseriousness; each can exist without the other.
reasons.opus: Both involve light, pleasant conversation, but charming is about winning others' liking, while lighthearted is a carefree disposition that treats everything lightly and need not be winning.

reasons.sonnet: Charming is about a winning, warm manner that makes one pleasant company, while agreeable here is about preserving harmony and avoiding conflict; they share pleasantness but differ in core focus.
Both concern pleasant social manner, but charming is about winning warmth and agreeable conversation, while polite is about observing courteous conventions; a person can be either without the other.
Charming is about a winning, agreeable social manner, while cheerful is about an inner disposition of good spirits; they share lightness and warmth but neither implies the other.

Both involve holding back until things are checked, but chary centres on withholding trust and keeping distance from people and offers, while cautious centres on risk awareness and gathering information before acting; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both describe holding back until one has checked, but chary centres on withholding trust from people and offers, while cautious centres on risk-awareness and gathering information before acting on plans.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve keeping distance from others, but chary is about cautious, trust-withholding vetting of new people and offers, while introverted is about social reserve, quietness, seriousness and low thrill-seeking, so they share only a loose core.

Both involve cautious holding back from risk, but chary is general wariness and withheld trust toward people and situations, while financially conservative is specifically about avoiding risk with money.

Both involve holding back from the unfamiliar, but chary centres on cautious scrutiny and withheld trust toward people and offers, while unadventurous centres on preferring routine and the familiar and avoiding novelty.
reasons.opus: Both hold back from the new, but chary is about wary distrust pending scrutiny, while unadventurous is a preference for routine and the familiar. Each adds something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve keeping distance from others, but chary is cautious, trust-withholding wariness toward new things, while reserved is emotional non-disclosure and polite distance; each adds something the other lacks.
reasons.opus: Both involve keeping distance, but chary is wariness and withholding trust until something is checked, while reserved is emotional non-disclosure and polite distance from everyone.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve hesitancy toward the new, but chary is a general cautious, distrustful guardedness toward people, offers and situations, while late-adopter is specifically about being slow to take up new technology or practices, possibly from inertia rather than caution.
reasons.opus: Both involve holding back from new things, but chary is general wariness and withheld trust, while late-adopter is specifically slow uptake of new technology or methods. Either can occur without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve easy, fluent talk, but chatterer is about idle, voluminous small talk while glib is about smooth, insincere, charming answers; neither implies the other.

Chatterer is about talking a lot of idle small talk, while laid-back is about a relaxed, low-stakes conversational manner; they share a casual tone but differ in core (volume of talk vs. ease/unhurriedness).
Both involve informal everyday talk, but chatterer is about talking a lot of idle small talk, while casual is about a relaxed, informal register regardless of amount or content.

Both involve casual, breezy speech, but chatterer is about constant idle talk on trivial topics while lighthearted is a general disposition of easy humor and not taking things heavily; neither implies the other.

Both involve producing too many words, but chattering is a quick, casual flow of small talk that fills silences, while verbose is long-winded elaboration in speech or writing; neither implies the other.
reasons.opus: Both are about excess words, but chattering is constant flowing small talk that fills silences, while verbose is padding a given point with elaboration, in writing too; each can occur without the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both describe constant, high-volume communication, but one is continuous spoken chatter filling silences while the other is frequent online posting and engagement, so they are neighbouring rather than the same concept.

Chattering is about talking constantly and filling silences, while stream-of-consciousness is about unstructured, associative flow of ideas; they share a rambling flow but each lacks what the other stresses.
Gemini includes talkativeness and sociability, but also adds wit, adaptability, changeability and superficiality, so it shares only part of the core with the stream-of-talk idea of chattering.
reasons.opus: Both centre on lively, quick talk, but Gemini adds information-gathering, adaptability, changeability and superficiality, while chattering is specifically incessant pause-filling speech.

reasons.sonnet: Both include fast, unceasing talk, but manic adds elation, racing ideas, high energy and grandiosity, while chattering is only about the steady stream of small talk.
Both involve a love of talk and sociability, but the 'Gemini' trait is a broader cluster that also includes wit, adaptability, changeability and superficiality, none of which chatty implies.
reasons.opus: Gemini includes a love of talk at its core but adds wit, adaptability, changeability and superficiality, while chatty is just about filling time with conversation; they overlap but neither implies the other.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve high-volume communication, but chatty is about enjoying spoken conversation, while frequent poster is about heavy presence in online forums and feeds; they overlap in the talkativeness core but each adds something distinct.
reasons.opus: Both describe a high volume of communicative output, but chatty is about enjoying spoken conversation for its own sake, while frequent poster is about constant online participation and visibility, so each has something the other lacks.

reasons.sonnet: Both involve verse-like, stylized language, but Chaucerian is a specific archaic, bawdy, satirical style while poetic is a general lyrical, imagery-rich style; neither implies the other.
